papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Do Natural Language Descriptions of Model Activations Convey Privileged Information?
papers.research_question: Do natural language descriptions of model activations (verbalization) provide privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, or do they mainly convey input information and the verbalizer's own knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that existing verbalization methods often do not convey privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, but instead reflect input information or the verbalizer's own knowledge, highlighting the need for better benchmarks and controls.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
For feature extraction datasets, a zero-shot baseline achieves high accuracy without access to activations, suggesting privileged knowledge may not be necessary for verbalization to succeed.
Prediction on reconstructed text (via inversion) matches verbalization performance, indicating tasks may elicit input text information rather than privileged knowledge.
Verbalizers often rely on their own world knowledge, especially when there is a mismatch between target and verbalizer knowledge, as shown in PersonaQA experiments.
Verbalization is sensitive to prompt phrasing, complicating interpretation of verbalizer outputs.
future_direction: Developing better benchmarks and experimental controls to assess verbalization methods.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability methods have proposed to translate LLM internal representations into natural language descriptions using a second verbalizer LLM. This is intended to illuminate how the target model represents and operates on inputs. But do such activation verbalization approaches actually provide privileged knowledge about the internal workings of the target model, or do they merely convey information about its inputs? We critically evaluate popular verbalization methods across datasets used in prior work and find that they can succeed at benchmarks without any access to target model internals, suggesting that these datasets may not be ideal for evaluating verbalization methods. We then run controlled experiments which reveal that verbalizations often reflect the parametric knowledge of the verbalizer LLM which generated them, rather than the knowledge of the target LLM whose activations are decoded. Taken together, our results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Levels of Analysis for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can methods from cognitive science, particularly David Marr's levels of analysis, be used to understand large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for understanding large language models by applying David Marr's three levels of analysis (computational, algorithmic, implementation) from cognitive science, and surveys established cognitive science techniques relevant to each level.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the levels of analysis framework and the toolkit of cognitive science methods provide a valuable approach for understanding the behavior and internal organization of large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models exhibit 'embers of autoregression'—behavioral trends that reflect their next-token prediction training objective, even in deterministic tasks.
LLMs show systematic deviations from normative benchmarks such as the axioms of probability theory, similar to human biases.
Methods from cognitive psychology, such as adapted implicit association tests, can reveal hidden associations in value-aligned LLMs that are not apparent in direct questioning.
At the implementation level, techniques like activation patching and circuit discovery can identify causal mechanisms within the model's architecture.
The levels of analysis framework provides a structured toolkit for making sense of LLMs by connecting their function, algorithms, and physical implementation.
papers.abstract: Modern artificial intelligence systems, such as large language models, are increasingly powerful but also increasingly hard to understand. Recognizing this problem as analogous to the historical difficulties in understanding the human mind, we argue that methods developed in cognitive science can be useful for understanding large language models. We propose a framework for applying these methods based on the levels of analysis that David Marr proposed for studying information processing systems. By revisiting established cognitive science techniques relevant to each level and illustrating their potential to yield insights into the behavior and internal organization of large language models, we aim to provide a toolkit for making sense of these new kinds of minds.

papers.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s "Interpretability Illusion" Arguments
papers.research_question: Are the phenomena identified by Makelov et al. (2023) as 'interpretability illusions' actually inherent properties of distributed representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the 'interpretability illusions' identified by Makelov et al. (2023) are not illusions but inherent properties of distributed representations, and provides additional experiments using DAS to analyze causal mechanisms in GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The phenomena labeled as 'interpretability illusions' are inherent to distributed representations, and the work by Makelov et al. (2023) has advanced the field of mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Even directions considered non-illusory by Makelov et al. can be classified as illusory under their own definition.
The illusions reported by Makelov et al. are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms.
DAS can reproduce and extend findings on the IOI task, showing that name position information in GPT-2 is distributed across attention heads and emerges in the 8th layer.
Name position information is not carried by MLP activations but by the self-attention block in the 8th layer.
The correct IO name representation is distributed across multiple attention heads in the 9th layer.
papers.abstract: We respond to the recent paper by Makelov et al. (2023), which reviews subspace interchange intervention methods like distributed alignment search (DAS; Geiger et al. 2023) and claims that these methods potentially cause "interpretability illusions". We first review Makelov et al. (2023)'s technical notion of what an "interpretability illusion" is, and then we show that even intuitive and desirable explanations can qualify as illusions in this sense. As a result, their method of discovering "illusions" can reject explanations they consider "non-illusory". We then argue that the illusions Makelov et al. (2023) see in practice are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms. We close by emphasizing that, though we disagree with their core characterization, Makelov et al. (2023)'s examples and discussion have undoubtedly pushed the field of interpretability forward.

papers.title: Towards Understanding In-Context Learning with Contrastive Demonstrations and Saliency Maps
papers.research_question: How do ground-truth labels, input distribution, and complementary explanations affect in-context learning performance in large language models when perturbed?
papers.core_contribution: This paper investigates how different components of in-context learning demonstrations affect model performance using saliency maps. It finds that label flipping impacts saliency more in larger models, input perturbations have smaller effects, and explanatory benefits vary by task.
papers.conclusion: The study uses XNLP techniques to show that label flipping reduces saliency, input neutralization has smaller impact, and complementary explanations are not beneficial for sentiment analysis, providing insights for understanding LLMs and curating demonstrations.
papers.key_findings:
Flipping ground-truth labels in demonstrations significantly affects model performance and saliency, with larger impact in larger LLMs like ChatGPT and InstructGPT compared to GPT-2.
Neutralizing sentiment-indicative terms in input has less impact on performance and saliency compared to changing ground-truth labels.
Complementary explanations do not improve performance for sentiment analysis tasks, unlike symbolic reasoning tasks, and their tokens are as salient as original input tokens.
Larger models exhibit emergent ability to override prior knowledge from pretraining when demonstration labels are flipped.
Saliency maps show that models pay less attention to flipped labels in smaller LMs but more in larger LMs.
papers.limitation:
Only 288 samples, only 20 examples for the saliency map and only 5 neighbors in the LIME model due to budget limitation and Openai daily request limit.
All the demos we used for the ICL is randomly selected, which will influence the model's accuracy performance in some cases.
We only pick the saliency map as the explanation method. In the future, more explanation models will support our conclusion better.
Unable to conduct the experiment on more complex tasks, such as grade school math problems, or common sense reasoning due to time-constrains and budget issues.
future_direction: Experiment with more LMs and more benchmark tasks and datasets to verify the findings of this study and make them more generalizable.
Investigate how demonstrations interact with the query test examples by adjusting exemplars in the demonstration based on their semantic distance from the query examples.
Compare gradient-based saliency map methods with perturbation-based ones and see how the saliency maps differ with the same input and model.
papers.abstract: We investigate the role of various demonstration components in the in-context learning (ICL) performance of large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we explore the impacts of ground-truth labels, input distribution, and complementary explanations, particularly when these are altered or perturbed. We build on previous work, which offers mixed findings on how these elements influence ICL. To probe these questions, we employ explainable NLP (XNLP) methods and utilize saliency maps of contrastive demonstrations for both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Our findings reveal that flipping ground-truth labels significantly affects the saliency, though it's more noticeable in larger LLMs. Our analysis of the input distribution at a granular level reveals that changing sentiment-indicative terms in a sentiment analysis task to neutral ones does not have as substantial an impact as altering ground-truth labels. Finally, we find that the effectiveness of complementary explanations in boosting ICL performance is task-dependent, with limited benefits seen in sentiment analysis tasks compared to symbolic reasoning tasks. These insights are critical for understanding the functionality of LLMs and guiding the development of effective demonstrations, which is increasingly relevant in light of the growing use of LLMs in applications such as ChatGPT. Our research code is publicly available at https://github.com/paihengxu/XICL.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Do You Trust Me? Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in narratives, where do these representations emerge across transformer depth, how well can they be decoded, and how do they relate to psychological constructs like fairness and certainty?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in systematic, layer- and head-specific patterns that are linearly decodable and align with psychological constructs like fairness and certainty, demonstrating that trust signals emerge during pretraining without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals, offering a representational foundation for designing credible and trustworthy AI systems in web applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences between high- and low-trust narratives are observed across models, indicating trust-sensitive features emerge during pretraining.
Trustworthiness is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, with probe performance varying by layer and head.
Fine-tuning with LoRA sharpens existing trust representations rather than restructuring them.
Trust representations are most strongly associated with psychological appraisals like fairness, certainty, and accountability-self.
Nonlinear probes provide only marginal gains, indicating trust information is largely in linearly accessible subspaces.
papers.abstract: Perceived trustworthiness underpins how users navigate online information, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs),increasingly embedded in search, recommendation, and conversational systems, represent this construct in psychologically coherent ways. We analyze how instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) encode perceived trustworthiness in web-like narratives using the PEACE-Reviews dataset annotated for cognitive appraisals, emotions, and behavioral intentions. Across models, systematic layer- and head-level activation differences distinguish high- from low-trust texts, revealing that trust cues are implicitly encoded during pretraining. Probing analyses show linearly de-codable trust signals and fine-tuning effects that refine rather than restructure these representations. Strongest associations emerge with appraisals of fairness, certainty, and accountability-self -- dimensions central to human trust formation online. These findings demonstrate that modern LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals without explicit supervision, offering a representational foundation for designing credible, transparent, and trust-worthy AI systems in the web ecosystem. Code and appendix are available at: https://github.com/GerardYeo/TrustworthinessLLM.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: ER-Test: Evaluating Explanation Regularization Methods for Language Models
papers.research_question: How does explanation regularization (ER) affect out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in language models, and how do different design choices (e.g., rationale alignment criterion, human rationale type, number of annotated instances, time budget) impact ER's effectiveness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ER-TEST, a framework for evaluating explanation regularization methods on out-of-distribution generalization, and provides insights into best practices for ER, such as the choice of rationale alignment criterion and human rationale type.
papers.conclusion: ER-TEST provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for ER methods, showing that ER improves OOD generalization and offering guidelines for effective ER usage.
papers.key_findings:
ER has little impact on in-distribution performance but yields large out-of-distribution performance gains.
The best ER criterion (e.g., MAE, Order) is task-dependent.
ER can improve OOD performance even with distantly-supervised (task-level) or few human rationales.
Rationale annotation is more time-efficient than label annotation for improving OOD performance when annotation time is limited.
ER-TEST enables comprehensive evaluation of ER methods across unseen datasets, contrast sets, and functional tests.
papers.abstract: By explaining how humans would solve a given task, human rationales can provide strong learning signal for neural language models (NLMs). Explanation regularization (ER) aims to improve NLM generalization by pushing the NLM’s machine rationales (Which input tokens did the NLM focus on?) to align with human rationales (Which input tokens would humans focus on). Though prior works primarily study ER via in-distribution (ID) evaluation, out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is often more critical in real-world scenarios, yet ER’s effect on OOD generalization has been underexplored.In this paper, we introduce ER-Test, a framework for evaluating ER models’ OOD generalization along three dimensions: unseen datasets, contrast set tests, and functional tests. Using ER-Test, we comprehensively analyze how ER models’ OOD generalization varies with the rationale alignment criterion (loss function), human rationale type (instance-level v/s task-level), number and choice of rationale-annotated instances, and time budget for rationale annotation. Across two tasks and six datasets, we show that ER has little impact on ID performance but yields large OOD performance gains, with the best ER criterion being task-dependent. Also, ER can improve OOD performance even with task-level or few human rationales. Finally, we find that rationale annotation is more time-efficient than label annotation for improving OOD performance. Our results with ER-Test help demonstrate ER’s utility and establish best practices for using ER effectively.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Does ChatGPT Have a Mind?
papers.research_question: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLMs have robust internal representations that satisfy various philosophical conditions, but the question of whether they have robust action dispositions for a full folk psychology remains open. It also contends that existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is strong evidence for LLM representation, but the question of whether they have full folk psychological states (beliefs and desires) remains open, particularly due to issues of action dispositions and stability.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs satisfy informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic conditions on mental representation.
LLMs exhibit internal representations that carry information about the world and are causally effective in generating behavior.
LLMs show evidence of world models and structured representations, such as in color and direction concepts.
The behavior of LLMs in game environments suggests they may have action dispositions, but the evidence is not decisive.
Skeptical challenges (sensory grounding, stochastic parrots, memorization) do not undermine the case for LLM representation.
papers.limitation: LLM outputs are very sensitive to prompting, which makes it hard to see the LLM as taking a wide range of means to promote a unified goal.
future_direction: Exploring how stable LLM outputs are to a range of different prompting environments.
Investigating whether LLMs have anything analogous to enduring goals or values.
Further research on how LLM strategies in game environments change under different prompting conditions.
papers.abstract: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions. We approach this question by investigating two key aspects: internal representations and dispositions to act. First, we survey various philosophical theories of representation, including informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic accounts, arguing that LLMs satisfy key conditions proposed by each. We draw on recent interpretability research in machine learning to support these claims. Second, we explore whether LLMs exhibit robust dispositions to perform actions, a necessary component of folk psychology. We consider two prominent philosophical traditions, interpretationism and representationalism, to assess LLM action dispositions. While we find evidence suggesting LLMs may satisfy some criteria for having a mind, particularly in game-theoretic environments, we conclude that the data remains inconclusive. Additionally, we reply to several skeptical challenges to LLM folk psychology, including issues of sensory grounding, the "stochastic parrots" argument, and concerns about memorization. Our paper has three main upshots. First, LLMs do have robust internal representations. Second, there is an open question to answer about whether LLMs have robust action dispositions. Third, existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.

papers.title: Explanations of Large Language Models Explain Language Representations in the Brain
papers.research_question: Are LLM-derived explanations effective in explaining language processing in the brain? Do the observed similarities between LLMs and the brain arise from shared pathways or are they simply artifacts of high-dimensional feature spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Attribution methods from explainable AI (XAI) can robustly predict brain activity during language processing, revealing a hierarchical alignment where early model layers correspond to early brain processing stages and later layers to higher-order stages.
papers.conclusion: XAI methods, particularly attribution, provide a powerful tool for linking LLMs and the brain, revealing shared computational principles for language processing and offering a brain-alignment framework for assessing explanation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution methods (Gradient Norm and Gradient × Input) predict brain activity across the language network, outperforming internal representations (activations, attention) in early language processing regions.
A hierarchical alignment exists: explanations from early LLM layers align with early brain processing areas (e.g., auditory cortex), while later layers align with higher-order areas (e.g., inferior frontal gyrus).
Layers with greater influence on next-word prediction (higher attribution scores) show stronger brain alignment, with a strong correlation between layer importance for prediction and brain alignment.
The predictive capability of attribution methods is consistent across participants and stories, and they encode brain-relevant information in a more compact representation compared to high-dimensional internal representations.
The study positions attribution methods as a powerful tool for bridging LLMs and the brain, offering a novel framework for evaluating XAI methods via neurobiological alignment.
future_direction: Examining a broader range of models, attribution techniques, and brain recording modalities to identify factors shaping alignment.
Extending the brain-explanation alignment approach to other cognitive domains (vision, auditory perception) and multimodal models.
Quantitatively comparing brain-based evaluation frameworks with traditional behavioral evaluation methods for XAI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) not only exhibit human-like performance but also share computational principles with the brain's language processing mechanisms. While prior research has focused on mapping LLMs' internal representations to neural activity, we propose a novel approach using explainable AI (XAI) to strengthen this link. Applying attribution methods, we quantify the influence of preceding words on LLMs' next-word predictions and use these explanations to predict fMRI data from participants listening to narratives. We find that attribution methods robustly predict brain activity across the language network, revealing a hierarchical pattern: explanations from early layers align with the brain's initial language processing stages, while later layers correspond to more advanced stages. Additionally, layers with greater influence on next-word prediction$\unicode{x2014}$reflected in higher attribution scores$\unicode{x2014}$demonstrate stronger brain alignment. These results underscore XAI's potential for exploring the neural basis of language and suggest brain alignment for assessing the biological plausibility of explanation methods.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Multimodal LLM Augmented Reasoning for Interpretable Visual Perception Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the applicability of Multimodal Large Language Models in visual perception analysis using principles from psychology and cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an annotation-free analytical framework to assess Multimodal LLMs for visual perception analysis, finding that visual clutter and simplicity principles correlate highly with human annotations, revealing biases in human perception.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that MLLMs can be used as cognitive assistants for interpretable visual perception analysis, paving the way for principled evaluation of their utility in HCI tasks and uncovering biases in human-annotated datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Visual clutter and the law of simplicity have the highest correlation with human annotations of visual complexity.
Different Gestalt principles impact various image categories differently; for example, law of closure correlates well with suprematism and paintings but not with advertisements.
The method shows consistent performance in the advertisement category across datasets, indicating robustness to biases.
Human-annotated datasets tend to overemphasize clutter and simplicity, influencing overall correlations.
MLLMs can provide interpretable assessments based on psychological principles without requiring annotated training data.
papers.limitation: Some MLLM models like LLaVa-NeXT and DeepSeek-VL had issues with consistent image ordering, and Llama 3.2 does not support multiple images in a single prompt.
future_direction: Evaluating the performance of different MLLMs like GPT 4v, Gemini Pro, etc.
Understanding the sensitivity of MLLM methods to the quality and design of the prompts.
Human-AI collaborations to refine MLLM reasoning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we advance the study of AI-augmented reasoning in the context of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), psychology and cognitive science, focusing on the critical task of visual perception. Specifically, we investigate the applicability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in this domain. To this end, we leverage established principles and explanations from psychology and cognitive science related to complexity in human visual perception. We use them as guiding principles for the MLLMs to compare and interprete visual content. Our study aims to benchmark MLLMs across various explainability principles relevant to visual perception. Unlike recent approaches that primarily employ advanced deep learning models to predict complexity metrics from visual content, our work does not seek to develop a mere new predictive model. Instead, we propose a novel annotation-free analytical framework to assess utility of MLLMs as cognitive assistants for HCI tasks, using visual perception as a case study. The primary goal is to pave the way for principled study in quantifying and evaluating the interpretability of MLLMs for applications in improving human reasoning capability and uncovering biases in existing perception datasets annotated by humans.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: From Latent Signals to Reflection Behavior: Tracing Meta-Cognitive Activation Trajectory in R1-Style LLMs
papers.abstract: R1-style LLMs have attracted growing attention for their capacity for self-reflection, yet the internal mechanisms underlying such behavior remain unclear. To bridge this gap, we anchor on the onset of reflection behavior and trace its layer-wise activation trajectory. Using the logit lens to read out token-level semantics, we uncover a structured progression: (i) Latent-control layers, where an approximate linear direction encodes the semantics of thinking budget; (ii) Semantic-pivot layers, where discourse-level cues, including turning-point and summarization cues, surface and dominate the probability mass; and (iii) Behavior-overt layers, where the likelihood of reflection-behavior tokens begins to rise until they become highly likely to be sampled. Moreover, our targeted interventions uncover a causal chain across these stages: prompt-level semantics modulate the projection of activations along latent-control directions, thereby inducing competition between turning-point and summarization cues in semantic-pivot layers, which in turn regulates the sampling likelihood of reflection-behavior tokens in behavior-overt layers. Collectively, our findings suggest a human-like meta-cognitive process-progressing from latent monitoring, to discourse-level regulation, and to finally overt self-reflection. Our analysis code can be found at https://github.com/DYR1/S3-CoT.

papers.title: Strong systematicity in sentence processing by simple recurrent networks
papers.research_question: Can simple recurrent networks display strong systematicity in sentence processing, i.e., process sentences with words in novel positions, without special architectural modifications or pre-arranged input representations?
papers.core_contribution: Simple recurrent networks can display strong systematicity in sentence processing without special architectural modifications or pre-arranged input representations, and this ability arises from informative word representations that develop in the network.
papers.conclusion: SRNs display strong systematicity, providing evidence against Fodor and Pylyshyn's claim that connectionist networks cannot display systematicity without implementing a symbol system, and that this systematicity arises from similarity-based representations.
papers.key_findings:
SRNs outperform smoothed best Markov models on test sentences requiring strong systematicity.
Hierarchical cluster analysis shows that SRNs group words based on abstract grammatical categories rather than exact grammatical roles.
The network's ability to display systematicity arises from the similarity of word representations in the input weight space.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on one simulation and further research is required.
future_direction: Investigate conditions that influence performance on tasks requiring strong systematicity.
Study how varying the number of animal nouns influences performance.
papers.abstract: Providing explanations of language comprehension requires models that describe language processing and display strong systematicity.Although various extensions of connectionist models have been suggested in order to account for this phenomenon, we found that even a simple recurrent network that had been trained in a way that can be considered 'standard', could display strong systematicity.This ability was found to result from informative word representations that developed in the network.

papers.title: Training Language Models to Explain Their Own Computations
papers.research_question: Can language models learn to faithfully describe their internal computations, and are they better at describing themselves than other models?
papers.core_contribution: Language models can be fine-tuned to generate faithful explanations of their internal computations, and they exhibit privileged access, meaning they explain themselves better than other models do.
papers.conclusion: Language models can be trained to explain their own computations via introspective interpretability, providing a scalable complement to existing interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning enables LMs to faithfully describe their internal features, outperforming zero-shot methods and nearest-neighbor baselines.
Self-explaining is highly data-efficient, achieving comparable results with only 0.8% of training data.
Privileged access is observed across three explanation tasks: feature descriptions, activation patching, and input ablation.
Explainer performance is correlated with activation similarity between the explainer and target models.
Models can generalize explanations to new features and feature bases, including full activations and activation differences.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on existing interpretability methods for supervision, which may be noisy or incomplete.
Only residual stream features are explained; other components like attention heads are not considered.
The explainer is trained on a fixed target model; adapting to continuously updated models is an open challenge.
future_direction: Extend explanations to other model components such as attention heads.
Scale the approach to larger models.
Investigate generalization across different architectures.
papers.abstract: Can language models (LMs) learn to faithfully describe their internal computations? Are they better able to describe themselves than other models? We study the extent to which LMs' privileged access to their own internals can be leveraged to produce new techniques for explaining their behavior. Using existing interpretability techniques as a source of ground truth, we fine-tune LMs to generate natural language descriptions of (1) the information encoded by LM features, (2) the causal structure of LMs' internal activations, and (3) the influence of specific input tokens on LM outputs. When trained with only tens of thousands of example explanations, explainer models exhibit non-trivial generalization to new queries. This generalization appears partly attributable to explainer models' privileged access to their own internals: using a model to explain its own computations generally works better than using a *different* model to explain its computations (even if the explainer model is significantly more capable than the target). Our results suggest not only that LMs can learn to reliably explain their internal computations, but that such explanations offer a scalable complement to existing interpretability methods. Code and data at https://github.com/TransluceAI/introspective-interp

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs).
